header.incumbent: An unnamed payments provider whose support was a ticket form
header.tag_why: Halima chose the vendor that put named people and an on-call commitment for every major on-sale in the room, and dismissed our support tiers as 'a queue with a faster timer', even though the CTO's team preferred our platform.

messaging_changes.current_line: Support plans with tiered response times, up to 24/7 coverage.
messaging_changes.change: A name, not a queue. For your biggest on-sales you get a named person and a stated on-call commitment: someone who picks up. For buyers who run high-volume events, especially operations executives. Publish the commitment only once the team can staff it, and drop 'tiers' and 'response times' as headline terms.
messaging_changes.why: The COO answered our tiers pitch with 'a queue with a faster timer' and described the need as 'a name, not a queue' and 'someone who picks up', never using the word 'support'.

messaging_changes.change: New line and one-page asset for high-volume event buyers: 'On-sale morning, minute four: who's watching, who you call, and what happens next. Here is the plan, on paper, with the names on it.' Build the on-sale readiness plan template with the solutions engineer and use it in evaluations with operations executives.
messaging_changes.why: The COO asked to see on paper what we do on an on-sale morning ('who's watching, who she calls, what happens at minute four'), and we had no such artifact.

messaging_changes.current_line: Trusted by leading businesses; see our customer stories.
messaging_changes.change: For high-volume event and ticketing buyers, replace the logo-led 'see our customer stories' with a reference from a ticketing or on-sale customer who can say in their own words who picked up when it mattered. Lead with that person's account, not the logo wall.
messaging_changes.why: The rep said 'I had logos. I didn't have a person,' and the decider wanted a person's account of an on-sale rather than generic proof.

messaging_changes.current_line: Built for developers: launch payments fast with our APIs, docs and sandbox.
messaging_changes.change: Do not lead with the developer and technical story (APIs, sandbox, load tests) for operations-executive deciders. Keep it for the technical evaluator, and open with the customer's framing for the executive: 'I don't buy uptime, I buy what happens when it's down.'
messaging_changes.why: The sandbox load test went great with the CTO but drew a one-word 'good.' from the COO, who made the call alone and said she buys behaviour during failure, not uptime.

trigger.insight: The trigger was a support failure as much as a technical one: payments broke at minute four, and nobody answered for the rest of the on-sale. Failures had happened twice before without action, so what moved the company was executive visibility, not the outage itself. The buyer was set up from day one to value 'who answers' over 'how fast it runs', and we scoped the evaluation as a throughput problem.
trigger.messaging: Open with the on-sale failure scenario (what happens at minute four and who picks up) rather than generic reliability, because that is the moment that starts these evaluations.

decider.insight: Halima set the deadline and made the call, yet we treated the CTO as the buyer. She saw our best proof, the load test, only secondhand through Ben, and the one time we spoke to her directly (support plans) it fell flat. We were winning with the person who did not decide.
decider.messaging: Build a separate operations-executive track (on-call, escalation, on-sale readiness) so the COO-level buyer hears a story written for her and not relayed by the technical champion.

competitor.insight: The competitor won by showing people, not features, and the customer's questions changed from technical to 'who' right after that meeting. The commitment of on-call for every on-sale is only Ben's report of what the competitor said; Jordan's view that they over-promised is a guess he admits he cannot back up. The competitor is also never named in the review, so we don't know who this is.
competitor.messaging: Stop treating named people and on-call commitments as a competitor gimmick; plan to counter them with our own named team and a concrete commitment, not by calling theirs unrealistic.

message.insight: Our developer and technical story landed with engineers and got a one-word 'good' from the decider. The support pitch (M5, tiers and response times) was answered with a rebuttal that it's a queue with a faster timer, and Jordan let it run to the end rather than switching to a person or a plan. What got reactions was what the wrong audience cared about.
message.messaging: Retire the tiers-and-response-times framing as the lead support message (M5) and replace it with named people and a stated on-call commitment; keep M2 for the technical evaluator, not the executive.

decided.insight: Jordan's 'we were the favourite' rests on Ben's momentum, and Ben was not the decider; Halima's remark was when the gap became visible, not when it opened. Jordan's belief that the load test had won it is the assumption that cost the deal, and no one tested it with Halima. Be careful with 'better platform' (his closing line): it is the rep's opinion, and the customer's criterion was different.
decided.messaging: Stop using technical wins and champion enthusiasm as proxies for being ahead; qualify the decider's buying criterion before treating the deal as won.

gaps.insight: The gap was a packaged artifact, not a product capability: an on-sale plan we didn't have, and a ticketing reference who could say who picked up. Jordan says he could have built a plan with the solutions engineer, so this was a process and enablement gap more than a product gap. Logos (M8) were not enough because she wanted a person's account of an on-sale.
gaps.messaging: Create an on-sale readiness plan template and a ticketing reference customer who can speak to the support response, and use them in place of generic customer stories (M8) for high-volume events.

language.insight: The customer defined the need as a person and as behaviour during failure, and never used the word 'support' that our product category uses. Her uptime line also directly undercuts the core of what we led with. E34 and E36 are attributed to 'they', so we cannot be sure which person said them.
language.messaging: Rewrite support copy using the customer's words, such as 'a name, not a queue' and 'someone who picks up on on-sale morning', and drop 'tiers' and 'response times' as headline terms.

gaps.question: Who was the competitor, and what exactly did they commit to for on-sales?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Jordan for the competitor's name, and ask Ben whether the on-call commitment was in writing in the proposal or contract.

gaps.question: Did anyone talk to Halima about why she chose them, beyond the one-meeting decision?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Jordan whether Halima or the CEO gave a debrief, and ask Ben what she said about the choice and what would have changed it.

gaps.question: Did the CEO or others weigh in, and was price a factor at all?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Jordan what the pricing difference was, if any, and whether it came up in Halima's meeting.

gaps.question: Is the lost scope the entire payments stack?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Jordan whether Tixhaven moved all payments to the competitor or only part of the business.

close.rep_takeaway: Winning the CTO is not winning the deal. When the decider asks for something on paper (an on-sale plan) and you have the means to build it, build it that day instead of assuming your best technical proof covers it, and find out early what the person who signs buys on.
